brand_names: Descovy (note: Descovy contains a different form of tenofovir)
what_its_for: This medicine is used in two important ways: (1) To treat HIV-1 infection in adults and children — it is always used together with other HIV medicines, never alone. (2) To help prevent HIV infection (called PrEP or Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis) in adults and teenagers who do not have HIV but are at high risk of getting it, such as through sexual contact or injection drug use.
how_to_take: Take this medicine by mouth, with or without food. Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water. Try to take it at the same time every day so it becomes part of your routine. Do not stop taking it without talking to your doctor first — stopping suddenly can be harmful, especially if you also have hepatitis B.
dosing: The usual dose for adults and teenagers weighing at least 35 kg (about 77 lbs) is one tablet (200 mg emtricitabine / 300 mg tenofovir disoproxil) taken once daily. For children, the dose is based on body weight and will be determined by your doctor. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions for your dose.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if it is within 12 hours of when you normally take it. If it has been more than 12 hours, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at your regular time. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are on PrEP and miss doses often, talk to your doctor, as consistent daily use is very important for prevention to work.
storage: Store at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep the bottle tightly closed. Store in the original container and protect from moisture. Keep this medicine out of reach of children. Do not use it after the expiration date printed on the bottle.
what_to_avoid: Do not take other medicines that contain emtricitabine or tenofovir at the same time (such as Atripla, Complera, Stribild, Genvoya, or Odefsey) — this can lead to a dangerous overdose. Avoid taking antacids that contain aluminum or magnesium within 2 hours of your dose, as they may reduce how well the medicine works. Do not share this medication with others. If you are on PrEP, this medicine does not protect against other sexually transmitted infections — use condoms to lower your risk. Avoid heavy alcohol use, as it can affect your kidneys and liver.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or seek emergency care if you notice: unusual muscle pain or weakness, trouble breathing, stomach pain, nausea or vomiting, feeling cold or dizzy, or a fast or irregular heartbeat — these could be signs of a rare but serious condition called lactic acidosis. Also call your doctor if you notice: yellowing of your skin or eyes, dark urine, or extreme tiredness (signs of liver problems); decreased urination, swelling in your legs, or bone pain (signs of kidney or bone problems); or if you develop a skin rash. If you have hepatitis B and stop this medicine, your hepatitis B may suddenly get worse — contact your doctor immediately if this happens.
when_it_works: For HIV treatment: This medicine starts working right away to lower the amount of HIV in your blood (called your viral load), but it may take several weeks to months to reach an undetectable level. You will need regular blood tests to monitor your progress. For HIV prevention (PrEP): Studies show the medicine reaches protective levels in the body within about 7 days of daily use for blood and rectal tissue, and about 20 days for vaginal tissue. It is most effective when taken every day without missing doses.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. This medicine is generally considered safe during pregnancy and is commonly recommended for HIV-positive pregnant women. There is a pregnancy registry to monitor outcomes — ask your doctor about enrolling. Breastfeeding: Women with HIV should not breastfeed because HIV can be passed to the baby through breast milk. Kidney problems: Your doctor may need to adjust your dose or monitor your kidneys more closely if you have kidney disease. This medicine is not recommended if your kidneys are severely impaired. Older adults: Kidney function should be monitored more closely in older patients. Hepatitis B co-infection: If you also have hepatitis B, do not stop this medicine without medical guidance, as stopping suddenly can cause a serious hepatitis B flare-up.
